subject: history
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In which year was the Treaty of Versailles signed?
questions.explain: The Treaty of Versailles was signed in June 1919, imposing harsh terms on the new Weimar Republic.

questions.q: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles was commonly known as the:
questions.explain: Article 231 forced Germany to accept sole responsibility for causing the First World War.

questions.q: In which city did Hitler attempt a putsch (armed uprising) in November 1923?
questions.explain: The failed 1923 Munich (Beer Hall) Putsch led to Hitler's imprisonment, during which he wrote Mein Kampf.

questions.q: When did Hitler become Chancellor of Germany?
questions.explain: Hitler was appointed Chancellor on 30 January 1933 by President Hindenburg.

questions.q: In which year did the Night of the Long Knives take place, purging the SA leadership?
questions.explain: In June 1934 Hitler purged the SA, killing its leader Ernst Röhm and removing potential rivals.

questions.q: After 1945, into how many occupation zones was Germany divided?
questions.explain: Germany was split into four zones controlled by the USA, Britain, France and the USSR.

questions.q: In which year was the Berlin Wall built?
questions.explain: The Berlin Wall was constructed by the East German government in August 1961.

questions.q: In which year did the Berlin Wall fall?
questions.explain: The Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989, a key step towards reunification.

questions.q: Why did the Weimar Constitution's use of proportional representation create political problems?
options: It gave the President no powers at all
It produced many small parties and unstable coalition governments
It banned all political parties except one
It prevented anyone from voting until age 30
questions.explain: Proportional representation meant many parties gained seats, making stable majority governments difficult to form.

questions.q: What was a main cause of the 1923 hyperinflation in Germany?
options: The government printed vast amounts of money, partly to pay striking Ruhr workers
A sudden fall in the German population
Foreign banks refusing to lend gold
questions.explain: After the French occupied the Ruhr, the government printed money to support passive resistance, destroying the currency's value.

questions.q: How did the Enabling Act of 1933 strengthen Hitler's power?
options: It allowed him to make laws without the approval of the Reichstag
It made him President for life
It abolished the position of Chancellor
It gave the SA control of the army
questions.explain: The Enabling Act let Hitler pass laws without the Reichstag, effectively creating a dictatorship.

questions.q: Why was the Reichstag Fire of February 1933 significant for the Nazis?
options: It was used to justify emergency decrees that suppressed the Communists
It destroyed all records of the Treaty of Versailles
It forced Hindenburg to resign as President
questions.explain: Blaming the Communists, the Nazis used the fire to pass a decree removing civil liberties and arresting opponents.

questions.q: Why did Stalin order the Berlin Blockade in 1948?
options: To try to force the Western Allies out of Berlin, partly in response to a new West German currency
To start a full-scale invasion of France
questions.explain: Stalin blockaded West Berlin's land routes after the Allies introduced the Deutschmark, hoping to drive them out.

questions.q: What was the main reason the East German government built the Berlin Wall?
options: To stop East Germans fleeing to the West
To defend against a NATO invasion
To increase trade with West Berlin
To provide new housing for refugees
questions.explain: Millions had escaped to the West through Berlin, so the Wall was built to halt this damaging exodus.

questions.q: How did Mikhail Gorbachev's leadership of the USSR help lead to German reunification?
options: His reforms and reduced Soviet control encouraged change across Eastern Europe
He personally ordered the Wall to be rebuilt
He banned all elections in the GDR
questions.explain: Gorbachev's reforms and refusal to use force to prop up communist regimes allowed reform movements to succeed.

questions.q: What is meant by the term 'Wirtschaftswunder' in relation to West Germany?
options: Its rapid post-war economic recovery, or 'economic miracle'
The building of the Berlin Wall
The secret police network of the GDR
questions.explain: The Wirtschaftswunder was West Germany's remarkable economic growth and prosperity in the 1950s and 1960s.

questions.q: A resident of West Berlin in 1948-49 receives food and coal delivered by Allied aircraft. This describes:
options: The Night of the Long Knives
questions.explain: During the blockade, the Allies supplied West Berlin entirely by air in the Berlin Airlift of 1948-49.

questions.q: A German voter in 1932 is influenced by mass unemployment and economic collapse to support the Nazis. Which event best explains this economic crisis?
options: The Wall Street Crash and the Great Depression
The signing of the Locarno Treaties
questions.explain: The 1929 Wall Street Crash triggered a depression and soaring unemployment, boosting support for the Nazis.

questions.q: In 1990, the two German states and the four former occupying powers signed an agreement clearing the way for a united Germany. This is known as:
questions.explain: The Two Plus Four Treaty (1990) was signed by East and West Germany plus the USA, USSR, Britain and France, enabling reunification.

questions.q: In 1989, large numbers of East Germans escaped to the West by crossing which country's newly opened border with Austria?
questions.explain: When Hungary opened its border with Austria in 1989, thousands of East Germans used it as an escape route to the West.
